stageDescription: Why governance exists, and how risk, controls, accountability and oversight connect.
title: Responsible AI principles

stops.title: In one line
stops.contentMd:
## In one line

Responsible AI principles are the shared values every AI system should meet, such as fairness, transparency and accountability, which laws, standards and company controls then turn into enforceable rules.

## The answer to give when asked "What are the principles?"

Say the list, in this order, without explaining unless asked:

> **Fairness, transparency, explainability, accountability, privacy and data governance, security and robustness, safety, human oversight, and sustainability.**

Then one line of credibility: *"Most organisations adapt these from the OECD AI Principles, the EU's seven requirements for Trustworthy AI, or NIST's trustworthy characteristics."*

At EY you started with "the definition is still developing". The interviewer wanted the list. Lead with the list.

## Explained like you're 10

Your school gets a robot to pick which kids go on the class trip. What rules should it follow?

| Principle | The robot rule |
| --- | --- |
| Fairness | It can't pick kids because of their name, skin colour or where they live |
| Transparency | Everyone knows a robot is picking, not a teacher |
| Explainability | If you're not picked, you can ask "why?" and get a real reason |
| Accountability | A named teacher is responsible if the robot gets it wrong |
| Privacy | It only uses what it needs, and doesn't tell anyone your secrets |
| Security and robustness | A clever kid can't trick it into picking only their friends |
| Safety | It never makes a choice that could hurt someone |
| Human oversight | A teacher can check and overrule its choices |
| Sustainability | It doesn't waste huge amounts of electricity doing it |

That's the whole idea. Everything else in this tab is about how real organisations make those rules stick.

## Why principles exist

AI started making decisions about people (loans, jobs, benefits, policing) faster than laws could be written. Principles gave governments and companies a shared set of values to agree on first, then turn into law and controls later.

Principles are **soft law**: not binding on their own. They become binding when a law or standard adopts them. The EU AI Act's recitals point back to the EU's 2019 ethics guidelines; NIST and ISO 42001 build them into risk management.

| Year | Milestone | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2019 | EU High-Level Expert Group: Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (7 requirements) | The value base the EU AI Act was built on |
| 2019 | OECD AI Principles, adopted by member countries and endorsed by the G20; updated 2024 | First intergovernmental AI standard |
| 2021 | UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, adopted by all member states | The global baseline, including developing countries |
| 2023 | NIST AI RMF: 7 trustworthy characteristics | Principles inside a risk management method |
| 2023 | G7 Hiroshima AI Process: guiding principles and code of conduct for advanced AI | Principles for frontier model developers |
| 2025 | India: RBI FREE-AI (Aug) and MeitY AI Governance Guidelines (Nov), each with 7 sutras | India's version, relevant for Indian clients |

The lists differ in wording but agree on substance. That's why you can give one consolidated list in an interview.

## Level 1: Each principle in practice

| Principle | Plain meaning | What organisations actually do | The assessor's question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fairness | No unjustified differences in outcomes between groups | Fairness testing across protected groups, proxy checks, agreed thresholds | "Which groups did you test, with which metric, and who approved the result?" |
| Transparency | People know AI is involved and how it's used | AI disclosures, model cards, an AI inventory, public statements | "Would an affected person know AI was used?" |
| Explainability | A decision can be explained in terms the audience understands | Reason codes, SHAP or LIME, citations for GenAI | "Can you explain this specific decision to the customer?" |
| Accountability | A named person answers for the system and its outcomes | Owners in the inventory, RACI, approval records, audit trail | "Who signed this off, and who gets the call if it fails?" |
| Privacy and data governance | Personal data is lawful, minimal, protected and good quality | DPIAs, data minimisation, lineage, retention rules | "What personal data does it use, and on what lawful basis?" |
| Security and robustness | It resists attack and keeps working under unusual inputs | Threat modelling, red-teaming, input and output filters | "What happens if someone tries to trick it?" |
| Safety | It doesn't cause physical, financial or psychological harm | Harm assessment, guardrails, kill switches, incident response | "What's the worst it could do, and how do you stop it?" |
| Human oversight | A competent human can monitor, intervene and overrule | Human-in-the-loop design, override rights, training, override monitoring | "Can a human stop it, and do they actually check?" |
| Sustainability | Environmental and social impact is considered | Model size choices, energy reporting, societal impact review | "Is a model this large needed for this task?" |

### Three pairs people confuse

- **Transparency vs explainability.** Transparency: *that* AI is used and how the system works in general. Explainability: *why* this particular output happened. A chatbot label is transparency; a reason code on a declined loan is explainability.
- **Accountability vs responsibility.** Responsible people do the work (data scientists, control owners). The accountable person answers for the result, and there should be exactly one.
- **Safety vs security vs robustness.** Safety: it doesn't harm people. Security: it resists deliberate attack. Robustness: it keeps working when inputs are messy or unusual, even without an attacker.

## Level 2: The major frameworks compared

You don't need every list word for word. Know the count, the source and one distinctive feature of each. That alone signals depth.

| Framework | Count | The list | Distinctive feature |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OECD AI Principles (2019, updated 2024) | 5 values-based principles + 5 recommendations to governments | Inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; accountability | The first intergovernmental standard; its AI system definition was reused by the EU AI Act |
| EU HLEG Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (2019) | 7 requirements | Human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; accountability | The value base of the EU AI Act; followed in 2020 by an assessment checklist (ALTAI) |
| UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) | 4 values + 10 principles | Principles: proportionality and do no harm; safety and security; privacy and data protection; multi-stakeholder governance; responsibility and accountability; transparency and explainability; human oversight and determination; sustainability; awareness and literacy; fairness and non-discrimination | Global reach, including developing countries; adds AI literacy and sustainability |
| NIST AI RMF (2023) | 7 trustworthy characteristics | Valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed | Treats "valid and reliable" as the foundation; frames principles as risk to manage |
| India: MeitY guidelines and RBI FREE-AI (2025) | 7 sutras | Trust is the foundation; people first; innovation over restraint; fairness and equity; accountability; understandable by design; safety, resilience and sustainability | "Innovation over restraint": India deliberately avoids heavy regulation |
| Microsoft Responsible AI Standard | 6 principles | Fairness; reliability and safety; privacy and security; inclusiveness; transparency; accountability | A common example of a company turning principles into an internal standard |

### How to use this in an answer

"The frameworks differ in wording, but converge on the same core: fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, security, safety and human oversight. For an EU client I'd anchor on the HLEG seven because the AI Act builds on them. For an Indian bank, the RBI's seven sutras. And I'd map both into one control set so the client isn't running two programmes."

## Level 3: When principles clash

This is where interviews separate list-reciters from practitioners. Principles regularly pull against each other. The governance answer is never "pick the right one". It is: **make the trade-off explicit, decide it at the right level, record why, and monitor it.**

Like you're 10: the class robot must be fair, so it should check it isn't picking fewer girls. But privacy says it shouldn't know who's a girl. Both rules are good. A grown-up has to decide how to balance them, and write down why.

| Tension | Example | How to handle it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fairness vs privacy | You can't test for ethnic bias without ethnicity data, which you may not hold or be allowed to use | Collect only for testing, strictly necessary, separated and protected (the EU AI Act allows this narrowly); or use inferred or synthetic test sets |
| Explainability vs accuracy | A deep model predicts defaults better but can't be explained to a declined applicant | Match to impact: high-impact decisions lean towards explainable models or strong post-hoc explanations; record the choice |
| Transparency vs security | Publishing how a fraud model works helps fraudsters beat it | Layered transparency: full detail to regulators and auditors, general explanation to the public |
| Human oversight vs efficiency | Reviewing every decision is slow, and reviewers start rubber-stamping (automation bias) | Risk-based review: humans check low-confidence and high-impact cases; monitor override rates |
| Safety vs helpfulness | Strict guardrails make a chatbot refuse legitimate customer questions | Measure both: harmful-output rate and wrongful-refusal rate, with thresholds for each |
| Accountability vs privacy | Logs needed to trace decisions contain personal data | Retention limits, restricted access, pseudonymised logs |

**Interview line:** "Principles conflict in practice, so the control isn't choosing one. It's making sure the trade-off is decided by someone accountable, documented with the rationale, and monitored."

## Level 4: Turning principles into controls

A principle on a poster changes nothing. It becomes real when it climbs four rungs: a **requirement** someone must meet, a **control** that tests it, **evidence** that the control ran, and a **metric** that shows it over time. If any rung is missing, the principle exists only on paper. This is exactly what consulting firms are paid to build.

| Principle | Requirement (policy or standard) | Control | Evidence | Metric |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fairness | No unjustified outcome gap across protected groups beyond an agreed threshold | Fairness test before go-live and quarterly; proxy check | Signed test report | Outcome gap per group, trended |
| Transparency | Customers are told when they interact with AI | Disclosure checked at release review | Release checklist, screenshot | % of customer-facing AI with disclosure |
| Explainability | Customers can get the main reasons for an adverse decision | Reason codes generated and sample-checked | Sample review log | % of explanation requests answered on time |
| Accountability | Every AI system has one named accountable owner | Inventory reconciled quarterly | Inventory with owners | % of systems with a current owner |
| Human oversight | High-impact outputs reviewed by a trained human who can overrule | Override and verification rates monitored | Monitoring dashboard | Override rate; verification rate |
| Security | GenAI is tested against known attacks before go-live | Red-team evidence reviewed at the release gate | Red-team report, issue log | Open critical findings |

### Tools organisations use

- **Responsible AI impact assessment:** a questionnaire per use case covering each principle, done at intake and before go-live.
- **AI ethics or governance committee:** decides the trade-offs from Level 3 and the hard cases.
- **Model cards and system cards:** short documents stating purpose, data, performance, limits and known risks.
- **Training:** so staff know what each principle means in their job.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick an AI system you know (Help Hub, or any other). For 3 of the nine principles, write the full Level 4 ladder: the requirement, the control that tests it, the evidence that proves the control ran, and the metric that tracks it over time. Then pick one pair from the 'three pairs people confuse' list and explain, in your own words, which of the two your system actually has today.

stops.title: Level 5: Advanced debates
stops.contentMd:
## Level 5: Advanced debates

Use these to show depth once the basics are solid. One well-placed point beats a long list.

### 1. Fairness can't satisfy every definition at once

The 2016 COMPAS debate is the classic case. COMPAS was a US tool predicting reoffending. ProPublica found Black defendants who didn't reoffend were wrongly flagged high-risk more often than white defendants. The vendor replied that scores meant the same reoffending risk for both groups. **Both were true.** Researchers (Kleinberg and colleagues; Chouldechova) then showed that when groups have different base rates, a model can't be equally calibrated *and* have equal error rates for both.

Like you're 10: you can't make a test both "same pass mark for everyone" and "same number of mistakes for every group" if the groups studied different amounts. You have to choose which kind of fair matters most here.

**So what:** choosing a fairness metric is a values decision for accountable people, not a data-science default.

### 2. Explaining LLMs is genuinely hard

Tools like SHAP work for traditional models. For LLMs, an explanation the model gives of its own reasoning may not reflect how it actually produced the answer. Research into model internals (interpretability) is young. Practical substitutes: citations to sources (RAG), evaluation, and limiting LLMs to uses where a wrong answer can be caught.

### 3. Human oversight can become theatre

Putting a human "in the loop" doesn't help if they have no time, no information or no authority to disagree. People tend to defer to the machine (automation bias). Meaningful oversight needs competence, time, access to the reasons, and the power to overrule, and it should be monitored. Your Help Hub finding is exactly this.

### 4. Ethics washing

Publishing principles without controls lets an organisation look responsible without being responsible. Warning signs: no named owners, no metrics, no budget, and an ethics body that has never stopped or changed a project.

### 5. Accountability across the value chain

A foundation model provider, an integrator and a deploying bank each control part of the system. When it fails, each can point at the others (the "many hands" problem). Answer: contracts that allocate responsibilities, documentation passed down the chain, and the deployer staying accountable to its own customers.

### 6. Sustainability is hard to measure

Training and running large models uses significant energy and water, but providers rarely disclose figures consistently. Practical step: use the smallest model that meets the requirement.

## Real failures that shaped the principles

Each principle exists because something went wrong. Naming one real case per principle is the fastest way to sound experienced.

| Case | What happened | Principle broken | Control that would have caught it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Amazon recruiting tool (reported 2018) | A CV-screening model trained on 10 years of mostly male hires learned to downgrade CVs mentioning "women's". Amazon scrapped it | Fairness | Fairness testing on historical training data before use |
| Dutch childcare benefits scandal (2021) | A tax-authority risk model used nationality as a factor; thousands of families were wrongly accused of fraud. The government resigned in 2021 | Fairness, transparency, human oversight | Ban on protected attributes, explainable decisions, human review before penalties |
| Air Canada chatbot (2024) | The chatbot invented a bereavement-fare refund rule. Air Canada argued the chatbot was responsible for its own words; the tribunal rejected that and made the airline pay | Accountability | Grounding answers in approved policy, plus clear ownership. The closest real case to your Help Hub work |
| Clearview AI (Dutch fine, 2024) | Scraped billions of face photos from the internet without consent to build a recognition database; fined 30.5m euro by the Dutch regulator | Privacy | Lawful basis and DPIA before data collection. Now banned outright by EU AI Act Art 5(1)(e) |
| UK A-level grading (2020) | An exam-grading algorithm downgraded many teacher-predicted grades, hitting students from historically lower-scoring schools hardest; the government reversed it | Fairness, explainability | Impact assessment on affected groups; individual appeal route |
| Microsoft Tay (2016) | A chatbot learning from Twitter users was manipulated into posting offensive content and taken offline within a day | Security and robustness | Adversarial testing; no unfiltered learning from public input |
| Samsung staff and ChatGPT (2023) | Employees pasted confidential source code into a public chatbot; the company restricted GenAI use | Privacy, security | Acceptable-use policy, approved tools, data loss prevention |
| Robodebt, Australia (2016-2019) | An automated system sent debt notices based on flawed income averaging, with little human checking; a Royal Commission later found it unlawful | Human oversight, accountability | Human review of adverse decisions; legal review of the logic. (Automation, not ML, which shows the principles apply beyond AI) |

Cases without links are widely documented; check details before quoting figures.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick one real failure from the table (not Air Canada, since that one's already mapped to Help Hub) and write 3-4 sentences on which control, had it existed, would have caught the problem before it reached customers. Then write one sentence applying the COMPAS lesson ('both were true') to a fairness trade-off in a system you know.

stops.title: Applied to your CV
stops.contentMd:
## Applied to your CV

Every finding you made at Barclays was a principle failing in practice. Framing them this way turns "what are the principles?" from a recall test into proof of experience.

| Your finding | Principle | How to say it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Help Hub source link was optional on live calls | Human oversight | "The oversight existed on paper but nobody had to use it, so it wasn't meaningful oversight." |
| Help Hub knowledge base had no owners or update SLA | Accountability, reliability | "Nobody was accountable for whether the content was current, so a correct model could still give wrong answers." |
| Draft and superseded policies could be retrieved | Transparency, data governance | "Agents couldn't tell if guidance came from an approved policy." |
| Mortgage selector hid the AVM valuation | Explainability, transparency | "Customers couldn't see or challenge the AI output that decided their options. The fix added a breakdown and a query route." |
| Speech-to-text not tested across accents | Fairness | "If transcription is worse for some customers, their complaints and vulnerabilities get missed more often: a fairness issue hidden inside an accuracy one." |
| Agent ratings fed retraining unchecked | Accountability, fairness | "The model could learn to please agents rather than protect customers, and nobody was watching what it was learning." |
| Complaint threshold set by engineering | Accountability | "A risk-appetite decision was being made by default by the wrong people." |
| Vulnerability triggers defined without safeguarding input | Fairness, inclusiveness | "The model only recognised obvious vulnerability language, so less obvious cases were missed." |

### The 30-second answer combining both

"The core principles are fairness, transparency, explainability, accountability, privacy, security, safety, human oversight and sustainability. At Barclays I saw them fail in practice: on a RAG assistant, human oversight was optional and nobody owned the knowledge base, which is accountability; on a mortgage tool, customers couldn't see the valuation behind their options, which is explainability. My job was turning each of those into a control with an owner."

## Free videos and courses

Free only. Suggested path: 1, then 2, then chapters 3-6 of course 3, then the fairness and accountability modules of 4.

| # | Resource | Source | Format and length | Level | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Five Pillars of Trustworthy AI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aGwYtUzMQUk) | IBM presenter | Video, ~6 min | Beginner | Fairness, explainability, robustness, transparency, privacy, plus why trust needs people, process and tools |
| 2 | [Embrace responsible AI principles and practices](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/modules/embrace-responsible-ai-principles-practices) | Microsoft Learn | Self-paced module, 9 short units | Beginner | Written for business leaders: Microsoft's six principles and how to design a governance system around them |
| 3 | [Ethics of AI](https://ethics-of-ai.mooc.fi/) | University of Helsinki | Self-paced text course, 7 chapters | Core | Free. Chapters on non-maleficence, accountability, transparency, human rights, fairness and ethics in practice |
| 4 | [AI Ethics and Governance in Practice](https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules) | The Alan Turing Institute | 8 modules with activities and videos | Advanced | Separate modules on fairness, explainability, accountability, safety, sustainability and data stewardship, each with a sector case |
stops.artifactPrompt: Write your own 'principle failing in practice' table like the Barclays one above, with at least 3 rows drawn from your own work history (any role, not just Barclays): the finding or problem, the principle it maps to, and one sentence on how you'd say it in an interview.

stops.title: Interview questions
stops.contentMd:
## Interview questions

| Question | Crisp answer |
| --- | --- |
| What are the principles of responsible AI? | Fairness, transparency, explainability, accountability, privacy and data governance, security and robustness, safety, human oversight, sustainability. |
| Where do they come from? | Mainly the OECD AI Principles, the EU's seven requirements for Trustworthy AI, UNESCO's Recommendation, and NIST's seven trustworthy characteristics. In India, the RBI and MeitY seven sutras. |
| Transparency vs explainability? | Transparency: people know AI is used and how the system works generally. Explainability: why this specific output happened. |
| Which principle is most important? | Accountability, because without a named owner none of the others gets enforced. (Then name one control.) |
| How do you operationalise a principle? | Turn it into a requirement, a control that tests it, evidence the control ran, and a metric over time. |
| Give an example of principles conflicting | Fairness vs privacy: you can't test for ethnic bias without ethnicity data. Decide at the right level, use the data only for testing, document it. |
| What's ethics washing? | Publishing principles without owners, controls, metrics or any power to stop a project. |
| A real case where a principle failed? | Air Canada (2024): its chatbot invented a refund policy, the airline said the bot was responsible, and the tribunal held the airline accountable. |
| Can a model be fair by every definition? | No. When groups have different base rates, you can't have equal calibration and equal error rates at once (the COMPAS debate). Choosing is a values decision. |
| Is a human in the loop enough? | Only if they have time, information, competence and authority to overrule, and you monitor that they do. Otherwise it's oversight theatre. |

quiz.question: What are the principles of responsible AI?
quiz.answer: Fairness, transparency, explainability, accountability, privacy and data governance, security and robustness, safety, human oversight, sustainability.
quiz.explanation: The nine-item consolidated list — lead with this, don't hedge.

quiz.question: Where do these principles come from?
quiz.answer: Mainly the OECD AI Principles, the EU's seven requirements for Trustworthy AI, UNESCO's Recommendation, and NIST's seven trustworthy characteristics. In India, the RBI and MeitY seven sutras.
quiz.explanation: Naming sources, not just the list, signals you understand these are adapted from real standards.

quiz.question: Transparency vs explainability — what's the difference?
quiz.answer: Transparency: people know AI is used and how the system works generally. Explainability: why this specific output happened.
quiz.explanation: One of the most commonly confused pairs — a chatbot label is transparency, a reason code is explainability.

quiz.question: Which principle is most important?
quiz.answer: Accountability, because without a named owner none of the others gets enforced. (Then name one concrete control.)
quiz.explanation: A values answer with a control attached beats a values answer alone.

quiz.question: How do you operationalise a principle?
quiz.answer: Turn it into a requirement, a control that tests it, evidence the control ran, and a metric that tracks it over time.
quiz.explanation: The four-rung ladder from Level 4 — a principle with any rung missing exists only on paper.

quiz.question: Give an example of principles conflicting.
quiz.answer: Fairness vs privacy: you can't test for ethnic bias without ethnicity data. Decide the trade-off at the right level, use the data only for testing, and document it.
quiz.explanation: Interviews separate list-reciters from practitioners exactly on this kind of question.

quiz.question: What's ethics washing?
quiz.answer: Publishing principles without owners, controls, metrics, or any power to stop a project.
quiz.explanation: Warning signs: no named owners, no metrics, no budget, an ethics body that's never stopped anything.

quiz.question: Give a real case where a principle failed.
quiz.answer: Air Canada (2024): its chatbot invented a refund policy, the airline argued the bot was responsible for its own words, and the tribunal rejected that and held the airline accountable.
quiz.explanation: The closest real case to RAG-assistant work like Help Hub.

quiz.question: Can a model be fair by every definition at once?
quiz.answer: No. When groups have different base rates, you can't have equal calibration and equal error rates at once (the COMPAS debate). Choosing which fairness metric matters is a values decision.
quiz.explanation: A mathematical constraint, not a modelling failure — important to say explicitly.

quiz.question: Is a human in the loop enough for meaningful oversight?
quiz.answer: Only if they have time, information, competence and authority to overrule, and someone monitors that they actually do. Otherwise it's oversight theatre.
quiz.explanation: People default to trusting the machine (automation bias) unless oversight is deliberately designed to counter that.

stops.artifactPrompt: Record yourself answering 3 of these 10 questions out loud, unscripted, in under 30 seconds each. Note which ones you fumbled or hedged on.

stops.title: Self-check
stops.contentMd:
## Self-check

Answer out loud before reading the answers.

1. Say the nine principles in under 10 seconds.
2. A bank labels its chatbot "AI assistant". Which principle does that satisfy, and which does it not?
3. Which framework is the EU AI Act built on, and how many requirements does it have?
4. Name India's framework for responsible AI in finance and its count of sutras.
5. Your Help Hub finding about the optional source link maps to which principle?
6. Why can't the fairness question in COMPAS be settled with more data?
7. What four things make human oversight meaningful?

**Answers:** (1) Fairness, transparency, explainability, accountability, privacy, security, safety, human oversight, sustainability. (2) Transparency yes; explainability no, because it doesn't explain any specific answer. (3) The EU HLEG Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI, 7 requirements. (4) RBI FREE-AI, 7 sutras. (5) Human oversight. (6) It's a mathematical conflict between fairness definitions, so people must choose which matters. (7) Time, information, competence, and authority to overrule.

quiz.question: Say the nine principles in under 10 seconds.
quiz.answer: Fairness, transparency, explainability, accountability, privacy, security, safety, human oversight, sustainability.
quiz.explanation: If you can't do this cold, nothing else in this module will stick under interview pressure.

quiz.question: A bank labels its chatbot "AI assistant". Which principle does that satisfy, and which does it not?
quiz.answer: Transparency, yes — people know they're talking to AI. Explainability, no — a label doesn't explain any specific answer the bot gives.
quiz.explanation: Tests whether you can actually apply the transparency/explainability distinction, not just recite it.

quiz.question: Which framework is the EU AI Act built on, and how many requirements does it have?
quiz.answer: The EU HLEG Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI, 7 requirements.
quiz.explanation: Knowing the lineage (ethics guidelines → recitals → Act) is what separates a sourced answer from a guessed one.

quiz.question: Name India's framework for responsible AI in finance and its count of sutras.
quiz.explanation: Relevant specifically for Indian-market clients or regulators.

quiz.question: Your Help Hub finding about the optional source link maps to which principle?
quiz.explanation: Oversight that exists on paper but nobody is required to use isn't meaningful oversight.

quiz.question: Why can't the fairness question in COMPAS be settled with more data?
quiz.answer: It's a mathematical conflict between fairness definitions (equal calibration vs equal error rates when base rates differ), so people must choose which one matters, not collect more data.
quiz.explanation: A structural limit, not a data or modelling problem.

quiz.question: What four things make human oversight meaningful?
quiz.answer: Time, information, competence, and authority to overrule — plus monitoring that the human actually uses all four.
quiz.explanation: Missing any one of these turns oversight into theatre.

stops.artifactPrompt: Write out your answers to all 7 self-check questions before revealing them. Note which ones you got wrong or hesitated on, and why.
